Clinical approach

  • Facts are easy to look up — the key skill is critical thinking and clinical recognition. Don't just memorise primary/secondary/tertiary: recognise how hypercalcaemia presents.

Hypercalcaemia — clinical features

Features (doctor)
Bones↑ bone resorption → osteoporosis; key clue: fracture after trivial trauma, especially in a young patient
StonesRecurrent calcium renal stones → look for hypercalcaemia (a single stone may not need a full work-up)
GroansAbdominal pain, constipation, bone/joint pain
Psychic moansFatigue, poor concentration, depression, forgetfulness of place ("where did I put my keys / park the car?") — forgetting names alone isn't specific
  • These are effects of hypercalcaemia, not specifically of hyperparathyroidism (one cause among many). With non-specific symptoms, look for hypercalcaemia first — not PTH first.
  • Initial screen for non-specific symptoms: CBC, TSH, electrolytes, corrected calcium.
Order matters: corrected calcium before PTH. Use corrected, not total, calcium.
  • Calcium 17 with lethargy and confusion (hypercalcaemic crisis) → IV fluids + loop diuretic. 439

Normocalcaemic hyperparathyroidism

  • High (or inappropriately high) PTH with calcium in the reference range — normal calcium does NOT exclude hyperparathyroidism. Calcium often sits near the upper limit (e.g. 2.35–2.36 if the limit is ~2.4 mmol/L).
  • Repeatedly high-normal calcium + compatible symptoms → revisit the history (abdominal pain, constipation, bone pain, forgetfulness, depression) and evaluate further. Hyperparathyroidism can worsen severe depression or even psychosis in predisposed patients.

Calcium, phosphate & magnesium

PTH-mediated hypercalcaemia: ↑ calcium, ↓ phosphate, ↑ (or inappropriately normal) PTH. High calcium + low phosphate justifies checking PTH.
  • Magnesium is linked to calcium physiology — refractory hypocalcaemia may need magnesium correction.
  • Reference ranges are population-based (~±2 SD). Interpret against the patient's own baseline and trend (e.g. a person whose systolic BP is always 80–85 may be normal for them).
  • Feature of primary hyperparathyroidism → hypophosphataemia 437; elevated PTH and high urine calcium. 439
  • Thyroid mass with high calcium and high PTH → primary hyperparathyroidism. 442
  • Calcitonin acting on the kidneys lowers plasma calcium (PTH and vitamin D raise it). 437 ×3

Types of hyperparathyroidism

TypePatternMechanism
Primary↑ PTH, ↑ Ca, ↓ PO₄Autonomous PTH from the gland(s) — adenoma (most), hyperplasia, carcinoma (rare)
Secondary↑ PTH (compensatory); Ca normal/lowVitamin D deficiency, CKD
Tertiary↑ PTH, ↑ CaAutonomous after long-standing secondary (CKD/dialysis)
  • High PTH, high Ca, low PO₄ + a small focus of uptake on sestamibi → parathyroid adenoma. 442 ×2
  • Hyperparathyroid symptoms 2 years after sleeve gastrectomy → vitamin D deficiency (secondary). 437
  • Dialysis patient with ↑ Ca, ↑ PO₄, ↑ PTH (tertiary) → total parathyroidectomy (± autotransplant). 437 ×2

Surgery for hyperparathyroidism (from past exams)

  • Before parathyroidectomy → localisation with a sestamibi scan (± US) 441; localisation is not mandatory but reduces the need for bilateral neck exploration (allows minimally invasive surgery). 442
  • Persistent disease 6 months after parathyroidectomy — missed ectopic inferior gland → within the thymus 442; a possible ectopic site (superior gland) → retro-oesophageal. 437
  • Sample for suspected parathyroid carcinoma → frozen section (intra-operative; FNA is avoided — seeding). 435

Post-thyroidectomy hypocalcaemia (from past exams)

  • Cramps, abdominal pain, brisk reflexes → hypocalcaemia 441 ×4; perioral tingling + Chvostek's → IV calcium gluconate 442 ×2; first action (keyed) → order a calcium level 437 ×3; Chvostek's sign 435 ×5; labs keyed low Ca, low PTH 441
  • After total thyroidectomy — not hypercalcaemia 427 ×2; a devascularised parathyroid can be autografted into the forearm. 439
dug:
• Usually associated with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis
  • Treatment: Chemotherapy & radiation, NOT surgery
Sarcomas & Metastatic Thyroid Tumors
  • Surgical excision if localized, but prognosis is poor.
  • Radiation and chemotherapy are often needed.

Parathyroid:

Parathyroid Glands: Embryology & Anatomy
Embryology
  • The parathyroid glands develop from the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches.
  • Superior parathyroid glands arise from the fourth pharyngeal pouch.
  • Inferior parathyroid glands arise from the third pharyngeal pouch (along with the thymus).
  • As they descend, they attach to the posterior capsule of the thyroid gland.
  • The inferior glands are more likely to be ectopic (in the thymus, mediastinum, or carotid sheath).
Normal Parathyroid Gland Anatomy
  • 85% of people have four parathyroid glands, but 15% may have more.
  • Located posteriorly on the thyroid, near the junction of the inferior thyroid artery and recurrent laryngeal nerve.
  • Superior glands: Found at the level of the cricoid cartilage, behind the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
  • Inferior glands: Found anterior to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, sometimes within the thyroid or thymus.
Appearance & Blood Supply
  • Color: Yellowish-brown
  • Size: ~2 × 3 × 7 mm
  • Weight: ~150 mg (for all four glands)
  • Blood supply: Primarily from the inferior thyroid artery but can also receive blood from the superior thyroid artery.
  • Cells:
  • Chief cells → Produce parathyroid hormone (PTH)
  • Oxyphil cells → Function unknown, increase with age
Physiology of Parathyroid Hormone (PTH) & Calcium Homeostasis

PTH, vitamin D, and calcitonin regulate calcium (Ca²⁺) and phosphate (PO₄³⁻) metabolism in bone, kidneys, and the gastrointestinal (GI) tract.

Role of PTH in Calcium Regulation
  • Secreted by: Chief cells of the parathyroid glands.
  • Trigger for secretion: ↓ Ionized calcium levels (Ca²⁺) in the blood.
  • Effect: Increases serum calcium by acting on: 1️- Bone → ↑ Osteoclast activity → Bone resorption → Ca²⁺ released into blood. 2️- Kidneys → - ↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption in the renal tubules. - ↓ Phosphate reabsorption (prevents calcium-phosphate precipitation). - Stimulates 1α-hydroxylase → ↑ Vitamin D activation. 3️- GI Tract → Indirectly increases Ca²⁺ absorption via activated vitamin D.
Vitamin D & PTH Interplay
  • Vitamin D (Calcitriol, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D₃) Increases intestinal Ca²⁺ & phosphate absorption. Inhibits PTH secretion via negative feedback. Promotes bone mineralization at normal Ca²⁺ levels.
Calcitonin & PTH Counter-Regulation
  • Secreted by: Parafollicular (C cells) of the thyroid gland.
  • Function: Opposes PTH by ↓ osteoclast activity, leading to ↓ Ca²⁺ levels.
  • Stimulated by: ↑ Serum Ca²⁺ levels.
  • Clinical relevance: Less critical in calcium homeostasis compared to PTH & vitamin D.
Diagnosing Parathyroid Disorders

Hyperparathyroidism: ↑ PTH + hypercalcemia without hypocalciuria.

Hypoparathyroidism: ↓ PTH + hypocalcemia.

Malignancy-related hypercalcemia: PTH-related peptide (PTHrP) secreted by

tumors (does not cross-react with PTH assays).

Primary Hyperparathyroidism (pHPT): Overview, Symptoms, and Diagnosis
General Overview
  • Cause: Excessive parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion despite normal or high calcium levels.
  • Most common cause of hypercalcemia in outpatients.
  • Peak incidence: 3rd-5th decades of life (more common in women).
  • Etiology:
  • Single parathyroid adenoma (85%)
  • Multiple gland hyperplasia (10%)
  • Parathyroid carcinoma (1%)
  • MEN 1 & MEN 2A syndromes
Symptoms & Clinical Features

Mnemonic: "Stones, Bones, Abdominal Groans, Psychic Moans, and Fatigue

Overtones"

1️- Kidney (Stones) → Nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, polyuria, polydipsia 2️- Bone (Bones) → Osteoporosis, osteitis fibrosa cystica, bone pain 3️- GI (Abdominal Groans) → Peptic ulcers, pancreatitis, nausea, constipation 4️- Neurologic (Psychic Moans & Fatigue Overtones) → Depression, fatigue,

confusion

5️- Cardiovascular → Hypertension, left ventricular hypertrophy 6️- Other: Band keratopathy, gout, pseudogout, chondrocalcinosis

Laboratory & Imaging Studies
  • ↑ Serum calcium (hypercalcemia)
  • ↑ PTH (inappropriately high or normal)
  • ↓ Serum phosphate (hypophosphatemia)
  • ↑ Urinary calcium (unless familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia [FHH] is suspected)
  • ↑ Serum chloride (hyperchloremic acidosis)
  • ↑ Alkaline phosphatase (if bone disease is present)
  • Bone X-ray → Subperiosteal bone resorption, cystic lesions, "salt-and- pepper" skull appearance.
  • DEXA scan → Osteopenia or osteoporosis.
  • Neck ultrasound & Sestamibi scan → Localize parathyroid adenomas.
Differential Diagnosis of Hypercalcemia

1️- Primary hyperparathyroidism (pHPT) → ↑ PTH + hypercalcemia 2️- Malignancy (Humoral Hypercalcemia of Malignancy, HHM) → ↓ PTH + high calcium (PTHrP-mediated) 3️- Familial Hypocalciuric Hypercalcemia (FHH) → Mild hypercalcemia + low

urinary calcium (<100 mg/24h)

4️- Milk-alkali syndrome → History of excessive calcium or antacid ingestion

5️- Hyperthyroidism → TSH suppression, increased bone turnover 6️- Sarcoidosis or granulomatous diseases → Increased 1,25 Vitamin D → ↑ Ca²⁺

absorption

7️- Vitamin D intoxication → Excess Vitamin D → Increased calcium absorption

Natural History & Complications
  • Untreated pHPT → Progressive bone loss, kidney stones, cardiovascular disease, pancreatitis.
  • Parathyroidectomy improves symptoms & reduces mortality risk.

Primary Hyperparathyroidism (pHPT) Treatment: Surgery & Management

Parathyroidectomy: The Only Curative Treatment
  • Surgery is the definitive treatment for pHPT.
  • Medical observation lacks strong evidence for long-term benefits.
  • Early intervention is preferred to prevent progression of complications (osteoporosis, kidney stones, hypertension, etc.).
Surgical Indications (Even in Asymptomatic Patients)
  • Serum calcium > 1 mg/dL above normal
  • Nephrolithiasis or hypercalciuria (> 400 mg/day)
  • Osteoporosis, fragility fractures, or vertebral compression fractures (T- score <= -2.5)
  • Age < 50 years
  • GFR < 60 mL/min
Hypercalcemic Crisis (Severe Hypercalcemia) Management

1️- Aggressive IV hydration (saline infusion) 2️- Correct electrolyte imbalances (hypokalemia, hyponatremia)

3️- Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) after hydration to promote calcium excretion 4️- Bisphosphonates (e.g., zoledronic acid, pamidronate) for long-term control 5️- Calcitonin for immediate but short-term calcium reduction 6️- Glucocorticoids (if hypercalcemia is due to vitamin D toxicity, sarcoidosis, or malignancy) 7️- Dialysis (if severe renal impairment or refractory hypercalcemia)

Preoperative Localization Studies

1️- Neck Ultrasound – Detects enlarged parathyroid glands & thyroid nodules 2️- Sestamibi Scan (Tc-99m) – Most commonly used; identifies hyperfunctioning glands 3️- 4D CT scan – More sensitive in reoperative cases 4️- Selective Venous Sampling for PTH – Used in complex cases or reoperations

Surgical Approaches
1️- Bilateral Neck Exploration (Traditional Approach)
  • Identifies all four glands
  • Used when localization studies are inconclusive
2️- Minimally Invasive Parathyroidectomy (Targeted Approach)
  • Smaller incision
  • Uses intraoperative PTH monitoring (PTH should drop >50% within 10-15 min post-excision)
  • Preferred for localized single-gland disease
3️- Reoperative Surgery (For Persistent/Recurrent pHPT)
  • Requires detailed localization studies (4D CT, venous sampling)
  • Higher risk of complications (nerve injury, hypocalcemia)
Postoperative Management & Complications
Hypocalcemia ("Hungry Bone Syndrome")
  • Occurs in patients with severe pre-op bone disease
  • Treatment: Oral calcium & vitamin D supplementation
  • IV calcium gluconate if severe symptoms develop
Persistent or Recurrent Hyperparathyroidism
  • Persistent pHPT → Calcium remains elevated within 6 months of surgery
  • Recurrent pHPT → Calcium normalizes but increases after 6 months
  • Requires reoperation with precise localization
Permanent Hypoparathyroidism (rare)
  • Requires lifelong calcium & vitamin D therapy
Follow-up & Long-Term Monitoring
  • Monitor serum calcium, PTH, and bone mineral density post-surgery
  • Most patients experience improved symptoms & quality of life post- parathyroidectomy
Surgical cure rate is >95%, with a low recurrence rate (<2%) in sporadic pHPT.
Secondary Hyperparathyroidism (sHPT)
Cause:
Compensatory PTH elevation due to chronic hypocalcemia, often seen in:
  • Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) (most common)
  • Vitamin D deficiency
  • Malabsorption syndromes (e.g., celiac disease, Crohn’s disease)
  • Rickets/Osteomalacia
Pathophysiology:

Bone disease (renal osteodystrophy) develops due to:

1️- Phosphate retention → Hyperphosphatemia suppresses calcium levels 2️- Reduced 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D → Decreased intestinal calcium absorption 3️- Parathyroid gland hyperplasia → Increased PTH release 4️- Skeletal resistance to PTH → Bone resorption continues, worsening osteoporosis

Clinical Features:
  • Bone pain & fractures (osteodystrophy)
  • Pruritus & soft tissue calcification
  • Vascular calcifications (calciphylaxis, tumoral calcinosis)
  • Increased risk of cardiovascular complications
Lab Findings:
  • Elevated: PTH & phosphorus
  • Low/NL: Calcium & Vitamin D (1,25-OH-D3)
  • Alkaline phosphatase elevated in bone disease
Management (Medical First-Line)
  • Vitamin D analogs (calcitriol, paricalcitol)
  • Phosphate binders (calcium acetate, sevelamer, lanthanum)
  • Cinacalcet (calcimimetic) to lower PTH
  • Maintain serum Ca × P product < 55 to prevent calciphylaxis
  • Dietary phosphate restriction + Dialysis
Indications for Surgery (Parathyroidectomy)
  • Persistent severe hyperparathyroidism despite medical therapy
  • Severe bone disease & fractures
  • Pruritus unresponsive to treatment
  • Extensive soft tissue calcifications
  • Calcium × Phosphate product > 70
  • Calciphylaxis (vascular calcification leading to skin necrosis)
Surgical Options:

Subtotal Parathyroidectomy → Remove 3️.5️ glands, leaving ~5️0 mg of normal tissue Total Parathyroidectomy + Autotransplantation → Parathyroid tissue reimplanted into the forearm or sternocleidomastoid muscle

Tertiary Hyperparathyroidism (tHPT)
Cause:

Autonomous, uncontrolled PTH secretion despite correction of underlying disease, typically after renal transplant

Pathophysiology:
Parathyroid glands become autonomously hyperplastic
Hypercalcemia develops despite normal renal function
Clinical Features:
  • Persistent hypercalcemia & bone disease despite kidney transplant
  • Nephrolithiasis (kidney stones)
  • Fractures & osteoporosis
Lab Findings:
  • Elevated: PTH & Calcium
  • Normal or Low: Phosphate (if kidneys are functional post-transplant)
Management:
  • Trial of medical therapy (Vitamin D, calcium, phosphate binders)
  • Wait at least 1 year post-transplant before considering surgery
  • Surgery (if hypercalcemia persists):
  • Subtotal Parathyroidectomy (3.5 glands removed)
  • Total Parathyroidectomy with Autotransplantation
Postoperative Considerations
  • "Hungry Bone Syndrome" → Marked calcium drop post-surgery due to increased bone remineralization
  • Requires aggressive calcium & vitamin D replacement
  • Close monitoring of calcium & PTH postoperatively
Hypoparathyroidism: Causes, Diagnosis, and Management
Overview

Hypoparathyroidism is a rare endocrine disorder characterized by low parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels, leading to hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia. It commonly occurs after thyroid or parathyroid surgery but can also be due to autoimmune or genetic causes.

Causes of Hypoparathyroidism
Surgical: Most common cause
  • Post-thyroidectomy (esp. for carcinoma or recurrent goiter)
  • Post-parathyroidectomy (accidental removal of all glands)
  • Neck radiation therapy
Autoimmune:
  • Idiopathic hypoparathyroidism (associated with Addison's disease, candidiasis, and other autoimmune disorders)
Genetic:
  • DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion) → Congenital absence of parathyroids
  • CaSR (calcium-sensing receptor) mutations → Leads to inappropriate PTH suppression
Other:
  • Magnesium deficiency → Impairs PTH secretion
  • Iron overload (hemochromatosis, thalassemia, Wilson’s disease) → Parathyroid gland damage
Clinical Presentation
Symptoms of Hypocalcemia (PTH Deficiency)
Neuromuscular
  • Tetany (muscle cramps, spasms)
  • Carpopedal spasm (Trousseau’s sign)
  • Facial twitching (Chvostek’s sign)
  • Laryngeal spasm → Stridor, respiratory distress
  • Seizures, convulsions
Neuropsychiatric
  • Paresthesia (circumoral, hands, feet)
  • Irritability, anxiety, depression
  • Cognitive dysfunction, psychosis
Skeletal & Soft Tissue
  • Brittle nails, dry skin, alopecia
  • Cataracts
  • Dental enamel defects (esp. if early-onset hypoparathyroidism)
Cardiac
  • Prolonged QT interval on ECG
  • Arrhythmias (rare but serious risk of sudden cardiac death)
Renal
  • Urinary frequency & polyuria
  • Nephrocalcinosis due to chronic hyperphosphatemia
Diagnosis
Key Laboratory Findings
  • Low: Serum calcium, PTH
  • High: Serum phosphate (due to decreased renal excretion)
  • Low or absent: Urinary calcium excretion
  • Normal or low: 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol)
  • Low magnesium (if present, can contribute to PTH suppression)
Imaging & Other Findings
  • X-ray/CT/MRI → Basal ganglia calcifications (due to chronic hypocalcemia)
  • ECG → Prolonged QT interval
  • Bone density → Osteosclerosis (paradoxically increased bone mass in chronic hypoparathyroidism)
Treatment & Management
Acute Hypocalcemia (Tetany, Seizures, Laryngospasm)
  • Medical Emergency – Immediate Calcium Repletion Required
  • Secure airway (laryngeal spasm may cause respiratory compromise)
  • IV Calcium Gluconate 10% (10–20 mL over 10 minutes)
  • Followed by IV calcium infusion (1–2 mg/kg/hr) in 5% dextrose
  • Monitor ECG (risk of arrhythmia)
  • Correct hypomagnesemia (MgSO₄ IV if Mg < 1.2 mg/dL)
  • Start oral calcium + vitamin D (calcitriol) once stable
Chronic Hypoparathyroidism
Goal: Maintain serum calcium in the low-normal range to prevent tetany &
avoid hypercalciuria
First-Line Treatment
  • Oral Calcium Carbonate or Citrate (1–3 g/day)
  • Vitamin D (Calcitriol 0.25–2 mcg/day) → Increases intestinal calcium absorption
  • Magnesium supplementation (if deficient)
Additional Treatments
  • Phosphate binders (e.g., sevelamer) → If persistent hyperphosphatemia
  • Low-phosphorus diet (limit dairy, processed foods, cola drinks)
  • Thiazide diuretics → Reduce urinary calcium loss
  • PTH Analog (Teriparatide) → For severe, refractory cases
Avoid Loop Diuretics (e.g., Furosemide) → Worsens hypocalcemia
Prognosis & Long-Term Considerations
  • Well-managed patients can live normal lives
  • Requires lifelong calcium & vitamin D monitoring
  • Monitor for nephrocalcinosis (calcium-phosphate deposition in kidneys)
  • Monitor for osteoporosis & cataracts
